note: An experiment (GAME_SPEC §6 Pistons, §13.7, Stage 79; docs/CURRICULUM.md, experiment 27) on data/benches/boyle.json: a sealed syringe of 100 mL of air pushed in and locked at 80 and 60 mL, its pressure and volume recorded at each: P V stands (Boyle's law).
title: Experiment: Boyle's law

steps.title: Your guess
steps.text: The syringe holds 100 mL of air at the room's pressure, 101 kPa, its nozzle capped. What will its pressure be, in kPa, squeezed to 60 mL? Type your guess, then click "predict".
steps.why: The same air in less room: its molecules hit each square centimetre of the walls more often.

steps.title: Lock its plunger
steps.text: Right-click the syringe, then click "lock plunger" in the column on the right.
steps.why: Locked, the plunger stays where your hand leaves it: a clamp holds it there, so the readings can be taken with your hand off it.

steps.title: At 100 mL
steps.text: Click "+ kPa" and "+ mL": the notebook records its pressure and where its plunger stands.

checks.text: its pressure and its volume recorded

steps.title: Push to 80 mL
steps.text: Drag its handle down to 80 mL on its scale and let go.
steps.why: Pushing takes force: the air pushes back on the plunger with its pressure over the room's on the plunger's area.

checks.text: its plunger at 80 mL, your hand off it

steps.title: Let it settle
steps.text: Wait for the air to come back to the room's temperature.
steps.why: Squeezing a gas warms it: work done on it is heat in it until its glass gives it to the room. Boyle's law is for the same temperature: read it once it is back at 20 C.

checks.text: the air back at the room's temperature

steps.title: At 80 mL
steps.text: Record its pressure and its volume again.

checks.text: its pressure and its volume recorded

steps.title: Push to 60 mL
steps.text: Drag its handle down to 60 mL and let go.
steps.why: It is harder now: the air's pressure has risen, and so has the force it takes.

checks.text: its plunger at 60 mL, your hand off it

steps.title: Let it settle
steps.text: Wait for the air to come back to the room's temperature.
steps.why: Squeezing a gas warms it: work done on it is heat in it until its glass gives it to the room. Boyle's law is for the same temperature: read it once it is back at 20 C.

checks.text: the air back at the room's temperature

steps.title: At 60 mL
steps.text: Record its pressure and its volume once more. Open the notebook and multiply each pressure by its volume.

checks.text: its pressure and its volume recorded

steps.why: P V is the same each time: halve the room, double the pressure, at the same temperature (Boyle, 1662). The scale reads the air under it; the nozzle holds about half a millilitre more, which makes the products agree better still.

goal.text: every element, mass and energy unchanged

report.label: the pressure at 60 mL
report.why: 101.3 kPa x 100 mL / 60 mL is 168.9 kPa; with the nozzle's half millilitre in both, 168.2 kPa.

report.label: P V at 60 mL
report.why: The same as at 100 mL: 101.3 kPa x 100 mL. A little under it by the nozzle's volume left out of the scale.
